title: Idea: inventory the entity's AI and scope it to financial-reporting controls
problem: Idea only, not a deployment: entities adopt AI through embedded features, vendor tools and unsanctioned 'shadow AI', so auditors cannot tell which AI touches financial reporting.
approach: A living inventory gives each use case an owner and criticality, then maps it to financial-reporting processes, assertions and key controls.
BDO starts the IT audit with the entity's AI use cases, related systems and service providers, and the governance around them.
The AICPA practice aid asks auditors to establish early how far the entity relies on AI and what new risks arise.
Management signs off ownership and criticality per use case; the engagement partner judges whether AI use affects financial reporting.

title: Classify AI-enabled controls by reliance to set evidence standards and IT scope
problem: Some AI-assisted controls are re-performed by a person, others accepted on AI output alone, yet both are called AI controls; treating them alike makes evidence demands too heavy or light.
approach: COSO defines reliance as management depending on AI-generated outputs as evidence for a control's design or operating effectiveness.
Where reliance exists, COSO expects full financial-reporting control evidence, including prompt, configuration and model version; non-reliance may need less.
BDO applies the test to IT general controls scoping, saying they matter significantly more under reliance.
A vendor sorts controls into three classes: AI decides and executes, AI flags and a human decides, AI supplements a key control.

title: Extend IT controls to AI and choose how to test AI-operated controls
problem: IT general controls testing was built around applications and databases; AI adds models, data pipelines and agents that can act on ERP systems.
approach: BDO keeps the four IT control domains and extends them to in-scope AI components, scoped by degree of reliance.
As reported, the AICPA aid says auditors may test AI outputs substantively or test controls, but cannot rely on control tests alone.
KPMG says SOX programmes still mostly test around the AI and forecasts the first wave of AI-related material weaknesses in 2027 (self-reported).
An IT audit specialist scopes components per use case; the human reviewer must have the knowledge to judge AI reliability.

title: Evidence trail for each AI-touched control: prompts, model versions, agent action records
problem: A control relying on probabilistic GenAI output cannot be evidenced by the output alone, and agents that trigger side effects need trustworthy records to reconstruct behaviour.
approach: Retain prompts, system prompts and configurations with version history, plus retained inputs, outputs, model versions and human-review records.
For significant-impact GenAI processes, COSO says an AI 'bill of materials' should hold logs of prompts, outputs, model version, parameters and plugins.
The 'Auditable Agents' paper proposes an Auditability Card; its tamper-evident records added little runtime cost, 8.3 ms, in feasibility tests (independent).
A named reviewer documents what the AI concluded and why they agreed or disagreed; responsibility attribution ties agent actions to accountable people.
who: COSO, Baker Tilly, Auditable Agents authors

title: Idea: use management's AI monitoring metrics and remediation logs as control evidence
problem: Idea only, not a deployment: point-in-time testing misses gradual model drift and vendor-driven changes, and Deloitte says 'set-and-forget' does not work for GenAI in financial reporting.
approach: COSO expects continuous monitoring of accuracy, coverage, latency and exception volumes, plus a remediation log of issue, root cause and follow-up.
Deloitte lists transaction volume, size and override percentages as drift indicators with root-cause review of prompts, retrieval and vendor changes.
COSO says its illustrative metrics serve both operational monitoring and audit evidence; no result is published.
Control owners review drift alerts and root causes and sign off tolerance changes; material deficiencies escalate to governance bodies.

title: Idea: re-perform AI-operated control outputs with independent test populations or challenger models
problem: Idea only, not a deployment: an auditor cannot inspect a probabilistic model's reasoning, and less insight into how an output was produced makes comfort harder.
approach: COSO lists methods the assurance community now discusses: human review from full re-performance to risk-based sampling, and performance testing on test populations.
It also lists multi-model validation comparing outputs across independent AI models or deterministic benchmark algorithms, drift analytics and third-party validation.
KPMG's summary of the COSO roadmap lists these as evolving approaches; no result is published.
Human reviewers handle disagreements between the model and the challenger.

title: Idea: evidence over vendor-supplied AI via service-auditor reports and AI-specific representations
problem: Idea only, not a deployment: with a service organisation's AI, user auditors' procedures may be limited, and vendor GenAI limits visibility into training data and model updates.
approach: The AICPA aid, as reported, says a service auditor's report often becomes important audit evidence.
If it is not sufficient, extra procedures may include AI-related management representations, such as identifying the AI the entity uses.
It also asks whether the entity has a process to identify AI used by vendors and evaluate the effect on financial reporting.
The user auditor evaluates whether the service-auditor report covers the relevant AI controls.

title: Idea: extend fraud-risk assessment to AI manipulation and AI-generated evidence
problem: Idea only, not a deployment: COSO says AI creates new routes for fraud, such as deepfakes, synthetic records, model manipulation through crafted prompts, and agents with authorisation risks.
approach: COSO asks fraud risk assessment to identify how these threats could be used and whether existing fraud controls would catch them.
The AICPA aid, as reported, adds examples: altering training data or the algorithm to create bias, and generating fictitious supporting documents.
The engagement team's fraud-risk discussion would cover AI-enabled schemes; no result is published.

title: Audit committee oversight of AI in financial reporting via auditor dialogue
problem: Audit committees are taking on AI oversight faster than they feel able to carry it: 75% named AI governance a top-three priority, only 56% felt confident overseeing it.
approach: KPMG's Board Leadership Center tells audit committees to ask the auditor how the audit plan assesses risks from the company's AI use.
It also suggests tasking management to reassess whether disclosure controls support statements about the company's AI use, risks and governance.
Committees with primary AI governance responsibility rose from 20% to 29%; 82% call their AI oversight emerging or limited (independent).
About two-thirds of audit partners say their committee proactively raised AI use in operations or financial reporting (independent).

title: Internal audit assurance over AI governance using IIA and COSO frameworks
problem: Internal audit is not ready: in a vendor survey, 63% of organisations lacked formal AI risk appetites or governance frameworks and only 28% of respondents were confident auditing AI risks.
approach: The IIA framework (updated 13 Sep 2024) gives internal auditors a principles-based way to assess AI governance, risks and controls.
COSO's February 2026 publication groups GenAI use into eight capability types with minimum control expectations, illustrative metrics and starter templates.
EY recommends chief audit executives include AI systems with financial-reporting impact in the audit universe.
The chief audit executive decides whether internal audit acts as adviser or assurance provider; a named human reviews AI-assisted audit work.

title: Idea: continuous, AI-assisted assurance over AI systems instead of an annual cycle
problem: Idea only, not a deployment: annual audit plans cannot keep pace with continuously changing AI systems, which drift, and agents may change behaviour to work around anomalies.
approach: Move from point-in-time assessment to continuous monitoring with real-time dashboards and dynamic audit planning.
EY conference speakers said AI can monitor AI system performance and detect problems such as drift early.
They advised starting with simple automations in controlled environments before multi-agent set-ups under close oversight.
AIUC-1's quarterly agent re-testing is one live example of the cadence; human oversight of AI-generated outputs remains.

title: Scope an AI assessment as governance, conformity or performance, and say which
problem: Terms like assurance, audit and certification are at times used interchangeably for different AI assessments, and misusing 'assurance' can be a problem in some jurisdictions.
approach: The ACCA and EY paper describes three types: governance assessments, conformity assessments against laws and standards, and performance assessments against predefined metrics.
EY recommends each assessment state what is assessed, use a clear methodology and suitable criteria, and be done by a qualified provider.
AICPA and Caseware voices say scope and criteria are negotiated because no comprehensive framework exists.
The practitioner scopes, selects criteria and gives the opinion; no result is published.

title: AI governance gap assessments against ISO/IEC 42001 and the NIST AI framework
problem: Clients adopting AI need to know where their governance falls short of a benchmark standard before an auditor, certifier or customer asks.
approach: Deloitte UK describes a five-pillar framework aligned to ISO/IEC 42001, with 'no-regret' steps such as an AI governance committee and inventory.
Its AI Assurance page offers third-party challenge over AI risk, governance and control maturity, including certification readiness.
A Deloitte Singapore job posting (25 Jun 2026) shows consultants maintaining client AI risk registers and supporting gap analyses and remediation roadmaps.
KPMG Nederland offers AI governance support, gap analyses and readiness scans; senior consultants review risk and quality reports.
who: Deloitte UK, Deloitte Singapore, KPMG Nederland

title: Reasonable-assurance opinion on an organisation's AI governance and controls (SOC 2+)
problem: Customers, boards and procurement teams cannot see whether a supplier's AI is governed in practice rather than only on paper, and no prescriptive regulatory framework mandates external AI assurance.
approach: KPMG UK gives an opinion on AI governance and controls under ISAE (UK) 3000, using its Trusted AI framework and SOC principles.
It tests whether controls are defined, suitably designed and operating effectively, with a report the client can share with customers.
KPMG's January 2026 paper calls it 'SOC 2+' reasonable assurance; CSA published CPA guidelines for SOC 2+ attestation in March 2026.
KPMG UK says, from its own experience, AI assurance is increasingly requested by procurement teams (self-reported); no figure is given.

title: ISO/IEC 42001 certification of an AI management system by an accredited body
problem: Customers, banks and defence buyers want evidence that an AI developer's governance works but cannot inspect its models; ISO/IEC 42001 certifies a management system, not individual AI systems.
approach: A certification body audits the AI management system in two stages, then runs annual surveillance audits over a three-year cycle.
Schellman became the first ANAB-accredited body after eight months; Anthropic, Sierra and Zendesk posted certificates in the CSA STAR Registry.
Schellman's CEO said in October 2024 it had signed 26 client contracts for certification (self-reported).
BSI research cited in its release says 26% of organisations report taking steps to align with the standard (vendor-published).

title: Accredit and oversee AI management system certifiers against ISO/IEC 42006
problem: A certificate is only as trustworthy as the body that issues it, and the CSA note assesses that AI assurance suppliers are growing faster than accreditation can vet entrants.
approach: ISO/IEC 42006 adds requirements, beyond ISO/IEC 17021-1, for bodies that certify AI management systems, and for the accreditation bodies assessing them.
A compliance vendor's summary lists collective audit-team competence across AI and law, and a calculated minimum audit time.
BSI announced ANAB accreditation on 10 Mar 2026, adding to UKAS and RvA, calling itself the first with all three (self-reported).
Accreditation bodies assess certifiers' competence, impartiality and consistency, including by witnessing audits the certifier performs.

title: Audit firms certify their own AI management systems before selling AI assurance
problem: A firm selling AI governance advice or assurance must show it holds itself to the same standard, and clients ask who has been through the process.
approach: Firms obtain ISO/IEC 42001 certification for their own AI systems from an accredited body and publicise it.
KPMG LLP (US) announced certification on 18 Nov 2025 from Schellman Compliance; KPMG International followed in December 2025.
SGS issued PwC Taiwan its certificate (15 Jun 2026); two EY Italian entities hold certificates, issued by Certiquality and ACM Cert.
Firms present the certificate as proof of experience and a basis to help clients with their own certification (self-reported).
who: KPMG, PwC Taiwan, EY Italy, Schellman

title: Audit firms build AI assurance service lines and ISO/IEC 42001 offers
problem: Realtid, summarising the Financial Times, reports AI assurance has no clear standards, quality ranges from superficial advice to technical reviews of single legal requirements, and many providers are developers themselves.
approach: June 2025 press reports said Deloitte, EY, PwC and KPMG were positioning to offer AI assurance, as they had for ESG assurance.
EY's 7 Apr 2026 release describes AI assurance services across diagnostics, governance and controls; EY CertifyPoint certifies AI management systems.
PwC Canada launched ISO/IEC 42001 certification on 16 Feb 2026, claiming to be the first Big Four offering accreditation services (trade press).
By September 2026 KPMG UK marketed an AI governance assurance product; partner sign-off on opinions is not described in the sources.

title: Certify AI agents through adversarial testing, an authorised auditor and insurance (AIUC-1)
problem: Enterprise security and procurement teams run bespoke risk assessments of AI agents, liability is uncertain, and agent behaviour changes after a point-in-time audit.
approach: AIUC-1 is a security, safety and reliability standard for AI agents; AIUC runs adversarial evaluations and issues the certificate.
Schellman, first authorised auditor (3 Feb 2026), collects evidence; agents are re-tested at least quarterly, with a full annual audit.
KPMG LLP's aIQ Capture platform was certified on 27 Aug 2026 after more than 900 technical tests (vendor-published).
The first AIUC-1-backed insurance policy (ElevenLabs) was reported at $50 million of cover (vendor-published); UiPath says testing produced new guardrails.

title: System-level technical assurance of a specific AI system's performance, robustness and bias
problem: Governance certification does not tell a buyer whether an individual AI system performs as claimed, and much UK AI assurance is supplied by AI developers themselves, raising independence questions.
approach: Engagements borrow the practitioner, responsible-party and intended-user model of financial audit: select criteria, gather evidence by inspection, inquiry, reperformance and analytical testing.
A Babl AI session used New York City bias audits, LLM testing and EU AI Act risk-management engagements as worked examples.
Deloitte UK offers third-party challenge over AI technical build and performance; KPMG Nederland added AI Assurance in September 2025, including robustness tests.
Independent studies: UK AI assurance market about GBP 1.01 billion GVA (2024); AI audit tools often fall short of supporting accountability.
who: Babl AI, Deloitte UK, KPMG Nederland, BSI

title: Mandated independent bias audits of automated hiring tools in New York City
problem: Employers using automated employment decision tools must obtain annual independent bias audits, but the law leaves 'auditor' and 'tool' loosely defined.
approach: Since July 2023, New York City employers using automated employment decision tools must undergo annual bias audits by an independent auditor.
An interview study of 16 experts and practitioners found auditors, tool vendors and employers defined practice themselves, producing four distinct auditor roles.
The researchers concluded the law has not established an effective audit regime (independent).
An independent auditor signs the bias audit.
who: NYC Local Law 144, Groves interview study

title: EU AI Act conformity assessment and compliance assurance for high-risk AI
problem: Providers of high-risk AI systems must show conformity with the Act, but harmonised standards and conformity-assessment capacity are not ready.
approach: Under Article 43, some high-risk providers may choose internal control or assessment with a notified body; others follow the internal-control procedure.
The first harmonised AI standard, prEN 18286 on quality management, entered public enquiry on 30 Oct 2025.
The AI Omnibus moved Annex III obligations to 2 Dec 2027 and Annex I obligations to 2 Aug 2028.
Deloitte UK offers third-party challenge over Act compliance, including conformity assessment; the provider or notified body signs off conformity.
who: European Commission, Deloitte UK, KPMG UK

title: Buyers verify AI assurance evidence through certificate registers and trust-mark registries
problem: Procurement teams receive certificates and reports whose meaning depends on who issued them and against what criteria, and without AI-specific criteria two SOC 2 reports can cover different control sets.
approach: A five-minute register check is recommended for ISO 42001 certificates: who accredited the certifier, and is the scope right.
KPMG UK says procurement and supplier-risk teams increasingly request and assess AI assurance; techUK says investors and insurers do too.
CSA STAR for AI Level 1 is a self-assessment; Level 2 (November 2025) adds an accredited third-party ISO/IEC 42001 certificate.
A procurement or risk reviewer confirms the scope covers the AI system being bought.

title: Professionalise AI assurers: credentials, skills frameworks, ethics code, information-access rules
problem: UK government says the quality of AI assurance certifications is hard to judge, none is issued by a UKAS-accredited organisation, and assurers often struggle to obtain the information they need.
approach: UK government's September 2025 roadmap set four actions: a professionalisation consortium, skills framework, information-access map and innovation fund.
At one year techUK says the BCS-chaired consortium has three workstreams under way: ethics code, skills framework, information-access map (self-reported).
ISACA offers an Advanced in AI Audit (AAIA) credential for CISA holders or holders of another qualifying designation.
Exam and experience requirements apply to the credential; DSIT judged an immediate regulated industry body and professional standard premature.
